title: Matrix-chain ordering: plain recursion vs dynamic programming
problem_statement: Given dimensions p_0, ..., p_n of a chain of n matrices (matrix i is p_(i-1) x p_i), compute the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to evaluate the product, over all parenthesisations.

algorithms.name: plain recursion
algorithms.idea: Try every top-level split point k and recurse on both halves, without memoisation.
algorithms.pseudocode: cost(i, j) = 0 if i = j else min over k of cost(i, k) + cost(k+1, j) + p_(i-1) p_k p_j
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(3^n) on every input: exactly 3^(n-1) calls and (3^(n-1) - 1)/2 split evaluations (n >= 1)
algorithms.correctness: Optimal substructure: the top split separates two independent subchains (PROOFS.md section 1; credit: CLRS). Running time: T(n) = sum_k (T(k) + T(n-k)) + Theta(n) gives T(n) - T(n-1) = 2 T(n-1) + Theta(1), so T(n) = Theta(3^n); PROOFS.md section 2 gives the exact counts.

algorithms.name: bottom-up dynamic programming
algorithms.idea: Fill m[i][j] for increasing chain length; each of the Theta(n^2) cells takes a min over O(n) split points.
algorithms.pseudocode: see implementation (bottom-up over the chain length)
algorithms.correctness: Bottom-up evaluation of the same recurrence; every split reads two shorter, already final subchains (PROOFS.md section 1; credit: CLRS).

relationship: Plain recursion is Theta(3^n) (full enumeration has Catalan(n-1) = Theta(4^n / n^1.5) parenthesisations, more than the recursion makes calls, from n = 18 on; PROOFS.md section 6); memoising the Theta(n^2) subchains gives Theta(n^3). Proofs of every claim: PROOFS.md. A published O(n log n) algorithm and a report on its correctness proof are background (cited; not implemented or verified here).

sources.title: Computation of Matrix Chain Products. Part II
Revisiting "Computation of Matrix Chain Products"
sources.note: Only the abstract (Crossref record) was consulted. It states that the correctness proof of Hu and Shing's O(N log N) algorithm is wrong and that the authors present an alternative proof for the correctness of the first two algorithms.

verification.method: V1: both agree on random chains with dimensions in [1, 50] (n <= 10 for recursion) and respect an independent upper bound. V2: runtimes fitted against 3^n and n^3 (measurements, not proofs). Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of the entry (correctness, the exact call and split counts, time, space, the count of parenthesisations); tests/test_proofs_matchain.py checks the computable facts on stated ranges, including both outputs against an explicit enumeration of all parenthesisations (n <= 9).

caveats: Dimensions are small integers, so arithmetic is unit cost.
notes: Hu and Shing's O(n log n) algorithm (see background) is not implemented or verified in this entry.

background.statement: Hu and Shing published an O(n log n) algorithm for matrix-chain ordering.
background.source: Hu & Shing 1982, 1984 (SIAM Journal on Computing 11(2) and 13(2)); abstracts of Parts I and II, checked against the Crossref records

background.statement: Schwartz and Weiss report that the original correctness proof of Hu and Shing's O(N log N) algorithm is wrong; their abstract states that they 'present an alternative proof for the correctness of the first two algorithms' they discuss.
background.source: Schwartz & Weiss 2019 (SIAM Journal on Computing 48(5)), abstract (only the abstract was consulted; checked against the Crossref record)
